title: Taming the ox
hookLine: fifth picture: patiently, the ox is tamed

lines: SEARCHING, TRACKS, A GLIMPSE, A ROPE.
cards: Every step so far has been about finding or grabbing. A search through the grass, tracks in the mud, a glimpse among green willows, a rope pulled tight as the ox bolted for the hills. The fifth picture is different.

Nothing is grabbed. It's about time. And it ties together a week that ran like one road, starting with Huineng: a robe no longer handed down, then meditation and wisdom as one, like a lamp and its light.

teach.b: First, one thought, then another. The preface, in paraphrase, says that when one thought arises, another follows right behind it. The ox wandering off isn't one big escape; it's a chain of small ones.
And the preface says these come up from the mind, not from the surroundings. The fields aren't the problem. The wandering is.
Second, keep the rope close. The verse says he keeps whip and rope near, in case the ox strays back into the dust. Not panic: the plain attention of someone who has done this every day for a while.
He no longer chases the ox across the valley. He notices the first step away and turns it back.
Third, gentle, it follows untied. Well tended, the verse says, the ox grows gentle and follows him on its own. No single great insight did that, no heroic effort.
Just the same small returning, again and again, until returning is the ox's habit too.

Fourth, patience is the method. Yesterday was grip; today is the long middle, the part of any practice that doesn't make a good story: the hundredth time back to the breath, the morning you sit anyway.
That's the week's thread. Huineng's lamp and light are one; the glimpse and the training aren't two.
The ox isn't tamed by force. It's tamed by being met, patiently, every time it wanders.

how: Zen students often describe their daily sitting with the language of the fifth oxherding picture: noticing the mind wander and returning it, over and over, as the slow work of training.

games.q: you're the herdsman. the ox takes one step toward the dusty road. it's the hundredth time today. what does the fifth picture suggest?
o: beat it into obedience once and for all.
games.why: the verse keeps whip and rope close but describes the ox growing gentle through steady tending, until it follows without a rope.

practice: Rest with the breath, and watch for the moment one thought hooks the next, the ox's first step toward the dust.

When you notice, come back gently, without a speech to yourself about wandering, and do it again, counting nothing, scoring nothing. Let the returning be easy, the way a hand keeps a rope loose but near.

wordCard.voice: Taming the ox. The fifth oxherding picture: through patient, daily attention, the wild ox grows gentle and follows without a rope. Today's word.
